p: The words 'in Ephesus' are missing from some of the oldest manuscripts, and the letter reads strangely without them.

readings.w: The Byzantine text and the SBLGNT (which prints the words in square brackets), and every other edition in this site's word list (NA28, NA27, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Textus Receptus); as listed on Wikipedia's page of Ephesians variants: Alexandrinus (A, 400s), the later correctors of Sinaiticus (01) and Vaticanus (03), the original hand of Claromontanus (D), many later manuscripts, and the Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Gothic and Armenian versions
readings.orig: τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν Ἐφέσῳ καὶ πιστοῖς
readings.en: to the saints who are in Ephesus and faithful
readings.plain: who are in Ephesus, faithful

readings.w: As listed on Wikipedia's page of Ephesians variants: P46 (about AD 200), the original hands of Sinaiticus (01, 300s) and Vaticanus (03, 300s), Minuscule 1739 (900s) and a corrector of Minuscule 424 (1000s). Basil of Caesarea (Against Eunomius 2.19) quotes the verse without the words and says that he found it so in old copies. Marcion's collection knew the letter as 'to the Laodiceans' (Tertullian, Against Marcion 5.11, 5.17)
readings.orig: τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς οὖσιν καὶ πιστοῖς
readings.en: to the saints who are also faithful
readings.plain: who are also faithful

why: The Plain English Translation keeps 'in Ephesus' because the Byzantine text and many other witnesses have it, and because Tertullian says the church's title for the letter was 'to the Ephesians'. But the oldest evidence is against it, so the reader should know the words may not be original.
b: Without the words, the Greek reads tois hagiois tois ousin kai pistois, "to the saints who are also faithful", and this is awkward: "who are" seems to need a place. Explanations: the original had a blank space for the name of each church, filled in as copies were made (a circular letter); "in Ephesus" was added when the letter was kept at Ephesus; Paul wrote to Laodicea and the copy to Colossae (Colossians 4:16 mentions a letter "from Laodicea"); or a later writer sent a general letter to Christians in Asia. Basil of Caesarea (Against Eunomius 2.19) says that in old copies he found the words absent. See also the note at 1:15.

p: The SBLGNT has 'Christ Jesus'; the Byzantine text, and the KJV, have 'Jesus Christ'.

readings.w: SBLGNT and NA28 (checked in this site's source texts)
readings.orig: Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ
readings.en: of Christ Jesus
readings.plain: of Christ Jesus

readings.w: Byzantine text (checked in this site's source text); the KJV reads 'Jesus Christ'
readings.orig: Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
readings.en: of Jesus Christ
readings.plain: of Jesus Christ

why: The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT order. The meaning is the same.
b: The two orders differ only in the order of the two words. The meaning does not change: "Christ" is a title (see the note at Romans 1:1) that had become part of the name.

a: and your love for all the saints
t: 'And your love for all the saints': in the oldest copies?
p: Some of the oldest manuscripts leave out the word 'love'.

readings.w: The Byzantine text and the SBLGNT (both checked in this site's source texts); most later witnesses, as the NET Bible's note on this verse says
readings.orig: καὶ τὴν ἀγάπην τὴν εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους
readings.en: and the love toward all the saints
readings.plain: and your love for all the saints

readings.w: As listed in the NET Bible's note on this verse: P46 (about AD 200), the original hand of Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (A), Vaticanus (B), and P, 33, 1739, 1881 and 2464
readings.orig: καὶ τὴν εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους
readings.en: and the [faith] toward all the saints
readings.plain: and toward all the saints

why: The Plain English Translation follows the longer text, which the Byzantine text and the SBLGNT both print. The NET Bible's note says the shorter reading has the stronger external support but is internally the harder one, because the saints would become an object of faith alongside the Lord Jesus, and that a scribe could have supplied the phrase from the parallel in Colossians 1:4.
b: The NET Bible's note on this verse lists the witnesses above and says that, externally, the shorter reading is superior. Internally it is a harder reading, since without "your love" the saints become an object of faith on a par with the Lord Jesus. A scribe could easily have supplied the phrase from the parallel in Colossians 1:4. The Plain English Translation keeps the longer text, which both editions in this site's source texts print.

a: This Spirit is a down payment
p: One letter changes whether the relative word agrees with the down payment or with the Spirit.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House and Westcott-Hort (checked in this site's word list; this reading agrees with the neuter word 'down payment', arrabon)
readings.orig: ὅ ἐστιν ἀρραβών
readings.en: which is a down payment
readings.plain: This Spirit is a down payment

readings.w: Byzantine text, Tregelles and the Textus Receptus (checked in this site's word list)
readings.orig: ὅς ἐστιν ἀρραβών
readings.en: who is a down payment
readings.plain: This Spirit is a down payment

why: The Plain English Translation follows the neuter 'which', which agrees with the word for down payment. Either way the sentence says that the Spirit is the down payment, so the English is the same.
b: The relative pronoun is ho (neuter, "which") in the SBLGNT and hos (masculine, "who") in the Byzantine text. The masculine agrees with the Spirit as a person, though the Greek word for Spirit is neuter; the neuter agrees with arrabon. The sense does not change.

p: The Plain English Translation reads 'in him'; the SBLGNT and the Byzantine text print the reflexive 'in himself'.

readings.w: NA28, NA27, Tyndale House and Tregelles (checked in this site's word list); the reading the Plain English Translation follows
readings.orig: ἐν αὐτῷ
readings.en: in him
readings.plain: in him one new humanity

readings.w: SBLGNT (ἐν αὑτῷ), Westcott-Hort, the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text (ἐν ἑαυτῷ), checked in this site's word list; the KJV reads 'in himself'
readings.orig: ἐν ἑαυτῷ (SBLGNT prints ἐν αὑτῷ)
readings.en: in himself
readings.plain: in himself one new humanity

why: The Plain English Translation reads 'in him', which matches the letter's refrain 'in him' and 'in Christ' (1:3-14; 2:13, 21-22). The SBLGNT and the Byzantine text print the reflexive 'in himself'; NA28 prints 'in him'. Either way the new humanity is created in Christ; the reflexive would stress that Christ is the one acting.
b: The Greek letters are the same either way: autoi ("in him") and hautoi ("in himself") differ only by a breathing mark, so the choice is the editor's. The reflexive reading points to Christ as the subject of the sentence; the other keeps the "in him" phrase that the letter loves. The Byzantine text spells the reflexive heautoi.

a: and peace for those who were near
p: The Byzantine text says 'peace' once; the SBLGNT says it twice, as in Isaiah 57:19.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles (checked in this site's word list)
readings.orig: καὶ εἰρήνην τοῖς ἐγγύς
readings.en: and peace to those who were near
readings.plain: and peace for those who were near

readings.w: Byzantine text (checked in this site's source text); the KJV reads 'and to them that were nigh'
readings.orig: καὶ τοῖς ἐγγύς
readings.en: and to those who were near
readings.plain: and for those who were near

why: The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT, which repeats 'peace' as Isaiah 57:19 does ('Peace, peace').
b: The meaning is unchanged, since 'peace' still governs the clause, but the repetition recalls the prophet's doubled word.

a: how the mystery became known to me through a revelation
p: The SBLGNT has a passive verb; the Byzantine text has an active verb with 'that'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles (checked in this site's word list)
readings.orig: κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν ἐγνωρίσθη μοι τὸ μυστήριον
readings.en: by revelation the mystery was made known to me
readings.plain: how the mystery became known to me through a revelation

readings.w: Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (checked in this site's word list); the KJV reads 'he made known unto me the mystery'
readings.orig: ὅτι κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν ἐγνώρισέν μοι τὸ μυστήριον
readings.en: that by revelation he made known to me the mystery
readings.plain: that through a revelation he made known to me the mystery

why: The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT passive. The active 'he made known' makes God the subject, and the Byzantine text adds 'that' before it.
b: The meaning is almost the same: either way the mystery was a gift from God by revelation.

p: The KJV adds 'by Jesus Christ' at the end of the verse; the SBLGNT does not.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles (checked in this site's word list)
readings.orig: τῷ τὰ πάντα κτίσαντι
readings.en: who created all things
readings.plain: the creator of all things

readings.w: Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (checked in this site's word list); the KJV reads 'by Jesus Christ'
readings.orig: τῷ τὰ πάντα κτίσαντι διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
readings.en: who created all things through Jesus Christ
readings.plain: the creator of all things through Jesus Christ

why: The Plain English Translation follows the shorter SBLGNT text. The longer reading says 'through Jesus Christ', words that echo Colossians 1:16 and John 1:3, where all things are made through him.
b: The doctrine that all things were made through Christ is found in Colossians 1:16 and John 1:3, but these words are not in the SBLGNT text of this verse.

p: The KJV adds 'of our Lord Jesus Christ' after 'Father'; the SBLGNT does not.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles (checked in this site's word list)
readings.orig: κάμπτω τὰ γόνατά μου πρὸς τὸν πατέρα
readings.en: I bend my knees to the Father
readings.plain: I kneel before the Father

readings.w: Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (checked in this site's word list); the KJV reads 'of our Lord Jesus Christ'
readings.orig: πρὸς τὸν πατέρα τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
readings.en: to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ
readings.plain: I kneel before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ

why: The Plain English Translation follows the shorter SBLGNT text. The longer one repeats a familiar phrase from 1:3.
b: The words "the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ" are the opening of 1:3, so they could be added here by memory. Without them 'the Father' is emphasized, in a verse about every family getting its name from him (3:15).

a: in the church and in Christ Jesus
t: 'In the church and in Christ Jesus' or 'in the church in Christ Jesus'?
p: The KJV has 'in the church by Christ Jesus'; the SBLGNT has an 'and'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles (checked in this site's word list)
readings.orig: ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ
readings.en: in the church and in Christ Jesus
readings.plain: in the church and in Christ Jesus

readings.w: Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (checked in this site's word list); the KJV reads 'in the church by Christ Jesus'
readings.orig: ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ
readings.en: in the church in Christ Jesus
readings.plain: in the church in Christ Jesus

why: The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT, with 'and', so glory is given in two places, the church and Christ Jesus.
b: With "and", glory is given in two places side by side: the church and Christ. The KJV's "by Christ Jesus" reads the phrase without the "and".
